title: Results
jupyter: python3
---

A run produces results: for each disease, the number of people in each state at each time point, and the number who made each transition in each step, plus any other quantities the model declares (prevalence, reported cases). This page covers what the results are, how to read them, how to change their time step, split them by group, compare them with data, plot them, and export them.

## Where results are

After a run, `sim.results` holds the results of each module by name, and the sim's own (such as `alive`, the population size):

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=10)) # 90% immune, 10 infectious

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()

res = sim.results.measles
print(res)
```

A disease has a result for each state (`S`, `I`, `R`: the number of people in it at each time point) and each transition (`infection`, `recovery`: the number who made it during each step), named after the variables they were made from. `res.I` and `res['I']` are the same.

## Reading a result

A result works like an array of numbers, one per time point, and also knows its time points, its label, and what kind of quantity it is:

```{python}
print('Peak infectious:', round(res.I.max()))
print('Total infections:', round(res.infection.sum()))
print('Infectious at the end:', round(res.I[-1]))
print('First time points:', res.I.timevec[:3])
```

Each result says how it is added up over time, as its `summarize_by`:

| Kind | `summarize_by` | What it is | Examples | Over a period |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stock | `'last'` | A number at each time point | `S`, `I`, `R` | The value at the end |
| Flow | `'sum'` | A number of events during each step | `infection`, `recovery`, `cases` | The total |
| Ratio | `'mean'` | One number divided by another | `prevalence` | Worked out again from the totals of its parts (the mean, for one with no parts) |

A result of your own gives it as `ss.Result('n_protected', summarize_by='last')`; if it isn't given, it is guessed from the name (`new_...` is summed, `n_...` and `cum_...` take the last value, and anything else is averaged), and `summarize_by=None` is for a result that isn't summarized over time.

A flow's running total is `.cum`, so `res.infection.cum[-1]` is the number of infections over the whole run.

### Time points

A result has one value for each time point of the sim, from `start` to `stop`. `I[0]` is the number infectious at the start, before any step; `infection[0]` is 0, since no step has ended yet; and `infection[1]` is the number of infections during the first step. A flow is dated at the end of its step: with daily steps, the infections dated 2 January are those during 1 January.

```{python}
print('Infectious at the start:', res.I[0])
print('Infections at the start:', res.infection[0])
print('Infections in the first step:', round(res.infection[1], 2))
```

## More results: ratios and outcomes

A model can declare more results. A ratio of states, such as prevalence, is given to the disease along with the transitions, and an outcome (`ss.outcome()`) is a quantity worked out from flows, such as the cases that are reported: here, half of infections, three days after they happen:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
N = S + I + R
infection  = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery   = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
prevalence = I / N                                   # The share of people infectious
cases      = ss.outcome(0.5*infection, delay=ss.days(3)) # Half of infections are reported, 3 days later
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, prevalence, cases, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=10))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles
sim.plot('measles')
```

Each result is named after its variable (`prevalence`, `cases`). See [Outcomes and observation](models_outcomes.qmd) for reporting, delays, and how long people stay in an outcome such as hospital.

## Changing the time step of a result

`resample()` gives a result over longer periods, adding it up by its `summarize_by` without being told: weekly cases are the total over each week, monthly numbers infectious are the value at the end of each month. `to_series()` gives a pandas series with the dates as its index:

```{python}
res.cases.resample('week').to_series().head()
```

```{python}
res.I.resample('month').to_series()
```

## Results by group

A disease stratified by age (see [Stratification](models_stratification.qmd)) still has one result for each state and transition; each is the total over the groups, and has the groups inside it. `select()` picks groups, and `by()` gives one line for each:

```{python}
by_age = measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}, inplace=False) # A stratified copy
sim = ss.Sim(by_age, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()

res = sim.results.measles
print('Peak infectious, all ages:', round(res.I.max()))
print('Peak infectious, aged 65+:', round(res.I.select(age='65+').max()))
res.I.by('age').plot()
```

A ratio such as prevalence is never averaged over groups: its numerator and denominator are each added up over the groups selected, and then divided. Here the groups mix at random, so the curves differ only by the size of each group; with a contact matrix, they differ in shape too.

A module written as code can keep its results by group too, rather than one result for each group (`prevalence_f_15_20` and so on). Stratify the sim, make the result with `groups=True`, and set it at each step from `sim.groups.count()`, which counts the people alive in each group for whom a condition holds, in one pass. As agents, stratifying by a property people already have, such as sex or age, changes nothing in the run, so it can be done for the results alone:

```{python}
class ByGroup(ss.Analyzer):
    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(ss.Result('prevalence', scale=False, groups=True))

    def step(self):
        groups = self.sim.groups
        self.results.prevalence.set_groups(self.ti, groups.count(self.sim.diseases.sis.I), groups.count()) # The infected over everyone, in each group

sim = ss.Sim(ss.SIS(), networks='random', analyzers=ByGroup(), stratify=dict(sex=['female', 'male'], age=[0, 15, 50]), stop=2010, verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.bygroup.prevalence.select(sex='female', age='15-49').plot()
```

## Comparing with data

Data is matched to results by name: a column called `cases` in a table given as `data=` is compared with the result `cases`, and plotted with it. Weekly data is compared with the total of the result over each week. Here the data is drawn from a run of the model itself with `sim.to_data()`, as weekly counts with random noise:

```{python}
truth = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', solver='binomial', rand_seed=2, verbose=0)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')
data.head()
```

```{python}
#| warning: false
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', data=data, verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles')
```

Data read from a file works the same way: `data=pd.read_csv('cases.csv')`, with a `date` column and a column named after the result. A column that matches no result gets a note listing the closest names. This is the data that [calibration](calibration_fitting.qmd) fits to.

## Plotting

`sim.plot()` plots the main results of every module; `sim.plot('measles')` those of one module, and `res.I.plot()` a single result. Each plot is labeled and dated from the results themselves.

```{python}
sim.results.measles.prevalence.plot()
```

## Summaries and export

`sim.summarize()` gives each result over the whole run, by its `summarize_by`: the total of a flow (`'sum'`), the final value of a stock (`'last'`), and the mean of a ratio (`'mean'`).

```{python}
sim.summarize()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## [PROPOSAL]
`sim.summarize()` should return the same kind of table as `msim.summarize()` (a dataframe with one `value` column, rounded for reading, leaving out results that are 0 throughout), so that one run and many runs read the same way (P15). Today it returns a dict of unrounded numbers, including results such as deaths that are 0 in a model without them.
:::

`to_df()` gives results as a table (a pandas dataframe), for one module or for the whole sim, with one column per result; it can then be saved with `df.to_csv()` or `df.to_excel()`:

```{python}
df = sim.to_df()
df.head()
```

`sim.results.flatten()` gives the same results as a flat dict, keyed like the columns (`measles_I`).

## Results of many runs

The runs of a stochastic model together (see [Uncertainty, seeds, and many runs](running_uncertainty.qmd)) have the same results as one run, with every run inside each. The usual summaries are built in:

```{python}
msim = sim.run(solver='binomial', n_runs=20)
res = msim.results.measles.I

median = res.median()            # The median of the runs at each time point
low, mid, high = res.quantiles() # The 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% quantiles at each time point
first = res.select(run=0)        # One run
res.plot()                       # The median, and the range of 95% of the runs
```

`msim.summarize()` gives the median and interval of each result over the whole run (the total infections of each run, for example), which is not the same as the median at each time point.

## Results with several columns

A result in a module written as code can have several values at each time point, such as new infections by variant; for a declared disease, [stratifying](#results-by-group) does this. A result made with `columns=` (`ss.Result('new_infections', columns=['children', 'adults'])`) has a column for each, available as `res.adults` or `res.col('adults')`, and each column is plotted, exported, scaled, and resampled as a result of its own. See [Analyzers](running_analyzers.qmd) for an example.

## Pitfalls

- **The flow at a time point is the step that ends there.** The peak in infections dated 10 March is the infections during 9 March, with daily steps.
- **A ratio is not a mean over groups.** Use `res.prevalence.select(age='65+')`, not the mean of the prevalence in each group.
- **Agents' results are scaled.** With each agent standing for several people, counts are multiplied by that number when the run ends; a count read in the middle of a run is in agents (see [Population rescaling](running_rescaling.qmd)).
